title: Matteo Ricci in China (1552–1610)
hook: a Jesuit who learned Chinese, dressed as a scholar and made friends

segments.voice: Yesterday, Galileo, told honestly: a condemnation, and much later a pope saying out loud that the Church had erred. Your line was the error, admitted. Did you get a chance to admit one of your own? Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

An Italian with a long beard sits in a scholar's silk robe, in a city at the far end of the world from Rome, and his guests are not there to hear a sermon. They're there for his maps, his clocks, his mathematics, and his memory, which could do tricks they had never seen. They argue with him about Confucius. He argues back, in their language, quoting their classics. Some of them become his friends. A few become Christians. His name is Matteo Ricci, a Jesuit, and the long word for what he was trying to do is today's word.
screen: `A SCHOLAR'S SILK ROBE.` → `MAPS, CLOCKS, MEMORY.` → `ARGUING IN THEIR LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Inculturation means letting the faith take root in a culture, speaking its language and wearing its clothes, without stopping being itself. Ricci never used the word. It came much later. But his life is one of the stories Catholics reach for when they explain it. First, the language. Ricci and his companions studied Chinese for years, the spoken language and the written characters, until he could write books that Chinese scholars read seriously. Second, the clothes. At first the Jesuits dressed like Buddhist monks. Then Ricci noticed who was listening: the educated class who read Confucius. So he changed into the robes of a scholar. Third, friendship. One of his early books in Chinese was a small collection of sayings on friendship, drawn from Western writers. It said, in effect: I came a long way, and I came to be your friend. One of his friends, the scholar Xu Guangqi, became a Christian and worked with him on translating geometry. Fourth, the hard question. Ricci judged that honoring Confucius and the ancestors could be kept by Chinese Christians as a civil and family custom, not worship. Others in the Church disagreed, strongly. That argument went on long after his death, and Church rulings on it changed over time. So inculturation is not a slogan. It's a question you have to keep asking: what belongs to the faith, and what is simply the coat it happened to arrive in? Paul put the instinct behind it in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "I became all things to all men, that I might save all."
screen: `FIRST, THE LANGUAGE.` · `FROM MONK'S ROBE TO SCHOLAR'S ROBE.` · `A BOOK ON FRIENDSHIP.` · `THE RITES: CUSTOM OR WORSHIP?` · then, large: `ALL THINGS TO ALL MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn something about another culture, the way a friend would. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you know whose family comes from somewhere you don't. A coworker, a neighbor, a classmate. What do you actually know about where they come from? A food, a holiday, a word? Notice where the knowing stops. Then pick one thing you'd like to ask them, not to study them, but because friends ask. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with curiosity. The bell holds the time.
Inculturation. The faith taking root in a culture, in its language and its clothes, while staying itself. Matteo Ricci, in a scholar's robe, is a story Catholics tell about it.
Your line: friendship first. Today, before you try to explain yourself to someone, ask them one real question about their world, and listen to the whole answer. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholic missionaries and bishops speak of inculturation when they bring the liturgy, music and art of a local culture into the life of the Church, and Ricci is often remembered in that conversation, especially by Jesuits.

Chinese rites: 'the popes ruled on it more than once, in different directions' summarizes the later condemnations and the later relaxation. Confirm it is fair and not overstated.
